The manufacturer describes stair climbing, uneven surfaces and tight-space maneuvering. These are qualitative mobility claims, not exact slope, clearance or all-weather test limits.

DogHouse is a separate protective, recharging and environmentally controlled hub. Its weatherproof enclosure and unspecified rapid charging do not establish the robot’s IP rating, charge duration or 24-hour battery life.

LTE/mesh networking, AES-256 encryption and redundant uplinks are advertised communication features. No independent penetration test, full data-flow assessment or cybersecurity certification is established.

Programmed/on-demand patrols remain monitored by human RSOC analysts who can intervene and escalate. 24/7 managed coverage, maintenance and replacement support are service claims, not guaranteed uninterrupted robot endurance or independently proven savings/crime reduction.

highlights: Security drone combines EO/IR sensing with DroneIQ flight management
DroneHome base supports automated landings and battery swaps
Remote RSOC operators monitor missions and can intervene
The exact Guardian page lists 35 mph aircraft top speed and IP45 weather rating. These are manufacturer ratings, not a ground robot’s speed or an independently inspected test certificate.

Flight duration is expressly worded up to 30+ minutes per mission. Payload, wind and test conditions are unspecified; the internally qualified wording is not converted into a guaranteed minimum or continuous multi-sortie runtime.

DroneHome supports automated launch/landing and battery swaps in less than three minutes. Swapping is not battery charging; repeated sorties and RSOC 24/7 staffing are not unlimited single-flight endurance.

Wind resistance is separately listed at 25 mph, distinct from the 35 mph aircraft top speed. EO/IR imaging, thermal detection and adverse-condition marketing do not establish independent detection accuracy or unrestricted all-weather operation.

The page advertises AES-256, redundant uplinks and LTE with optional Starlink integration. Starlink is not assumed standard; operator licensing and broad compliance language do not establish universal site-specific flight permission.

The manufacturer claims more than 45,000 completed automated patrol/alarm missions and calls Guardian the most widely used automated security drone system. The undated supplier total is not independently verified market share, per-aircraft throughput or a measured reliability/uptime guarantee.

highlights: Asylon’s current named ground and aerial systems are DroneDog and Guardian. DroneDog integrates Boston Dynamics Spot with the proprietary PupPack security payload; the integration is retained separately from bare Spot.

DogHouse charging/protection and DroneHome aerial launch/landing/battery swapping are support infrastructure. PupPack is a security payload, DroneIQ is software and RSOC is a staffed service; these labels are not additional whole robot models.

The company describes a Robotics-as-a-Service model integrating ground/aerial patrols, alarm/access-control/sensor interfaces, reporting, user permissions and human RSOC oversight. A service description does not establish numeric pricing or an exact deployment package.

24/7 monitoring, human intervention and battery infrastructure enable repeated missions. They do not establish 24-hour single-battery endurance, unconditional uptime, unrestricted autonomous operation or universal regulatory permission.

Savings, increased patrol counts, crime reduction, exclusivity and most-widely-used claims remain supplier positioning or testimonials, not independently established outcomes or market leadership. Company founding in 2015 is not either robot’s first-release year.
